opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, in the beginning success was pretty binary and pretty humble. The first question was simply: does the policy we trained in simulation do anything sensible at all when we put it on the real robot? For a long time the default outcome of sim-to-real transfer was that the robot would just shake, fall over, or behave in some strange way that exploited a quirk of the simulator. So the first milestone was getting ANYmal to stand up and walk on flat ground without us babysitting it.

Once that worked, the bar moved quickly. We started looking at robustness: can it handle terrain it never saw exactly in training, like stairs, slopes, gravel, or grass? Can it recover when you push it or when it slips? A big part of that work was training in massively parallel simulation, thousands of robots at once on the GPU, with a curriculum of increasingly difficult terrain. One really nice property of that setup is that the curriculum itself gives you a measure of progress. You can see how far up the difficulty levels the robots make it, how fast they get there, and whether they're tracking the commanded velocities.

But I'd say the real test was always the hardware. Simulation metrics are useful for iterating, but they can fool you. A policy can look great in sim and still be too aggressive, too jittery, or hard on the motors in reality. So we cared a lot about qualitative things too: does the motion look natural, is it smooth, would we trust it outside the lab? Taking the robot out on hikes or into unstructured environments, and having it just keep going, that's when you knew something had genuinely worked.

And another, more practical measure for us was training time. Going from days of training down to minutes changed how we worked. If you can train a walking policy in about twenty minutes, you can iterate on reward design and ideas so much faster, and that ended up being one of the most important outcomes of that early work.

r002.rationale: It describes faster training as an important practical outcome and mentions a walking policy trained in about twenty minutes, but does not identify reducing training time for basic locomotion as the central focus.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, in the early days success was defined pretty narrowly, and I think that was the right call at the time. The question we were asking was almost binary: can a policy trained entirely in simulation make a real quadruped walk, without falling over, when you take it out of the lab and put it on terrain it has never seen? So the first metric was just robustness. Does it stay up on stairs, on gravel, on slippery floors, when you push it? If the robot fell, nothing else mattered.

The second thing we cared about was training time, and that was a bit unusual. With Isaac Gym we could run thousands of environments in parallel on a single GPU, and we went from training runs that took days on CPU clusters to policies that were walking in simulation in minutes. That mattered to me not because speed is a goal in itself, but because it changed how we worked. If a run takes twenty minutes instead of two days, you iterate on reward design, on curriculum, on randomization, ten times faster. The quality of the final policy was really a function of how many ideas we could try.

And then the honest answer is that a lot of judging success was qualitative. We would look at the gait and ask, does this look like something a robot should do? Early on you get policies that technically meet the reward but move in these jittery, high-frequency ways that would destroy the hardware. So we spent a lot of effort on reward terms that penalized joint accelerations and torques, and the test was whether a policy that scored well in sim also looked healthy and transferred to the real ANYmal without us holding our breath. When that gap closed, when sim performance started being predictive of real performance, that's when I felt the approach was actually working rather than just a nice demo.

r001.rationale: The response describes success as walking robustly on unfamiliar terrain, but does not say that taking just a few steps counted as a major success.

r002.rationale: It discusses faster training as the second concern and as a way to iterate more quickly; it identifies robustness as the first metric, not reduced training time as the central focus.

astra-6.text: Early on, the main question was whether we could train a policy in simulation and then put it on the real robot and have it walk. A high reward in simulation wasn’t enough—the real test was whether the behavior transferred. Could the robot keep its balance and move as commanded, despite the differences between the simulator and the hardware? That was the key measure of success, rather than whether the gait looked particularly elegant.

The real test was whether the behavior transferred to hardware and remained stable despite differences between the simulation and the physical robot. Then we could start looking at how well it followed commands and handled disturbances.
